claims.title: Portuguese reach the Kingdom of Kongo
claims.summary: The navigator Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo River and made contact with the Kingdom of Kongo, opening relations between this powerful Central African monarchy and Portugal.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Angola: From the kingdoms of Kongo, Ndongo and Matamba and Queen Njinga's long resistance, through centuries as a heartland of the Atlantic slave trade and a slow colonial conquest, to a hard-won independence and an oil-rich modern republic forged out of decades of war.", terralore.co/country/AGO/chronicle#ev-1483-portuguese-reach-the-kingdom-of-kongo, claim TL:AGO:event:1483:portuguese-reach-the-kingdom-of-kongo, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Kongo adopts Christianity
claims.summary: The Kongo ruler was baptised and, under his son Afonso I, the kingdom embraced Catholicism, literacy and sustained diplomatic ties with Portugal and the papacy.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Angola: From the kingdoms of Kongo, Ndongo and Matamba and Queen Njinga's long resistance, through centuries as a heartland of the Atlantic slave trade and a slow colonial conquest, to a hard-won independence and an oil-rich modern republic forged out of decades of war.", terralore.co/country/AGO/chronicle#ev-1491-kongo-adopts-christianity, claim TL:AGO:event:1491:kongo-adopts-christianity, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Rise of Ndongo under the ngola
claims.summary: The Kimbundu-speaking Kingdom of Ndongo grew in strength under its ruler the ngola, asserting independence from Kongo; the title would give the future colony its name.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Angola: From the kingdoms of Kongo, Ndongo and Matamba and Queen Njinga's long resistance, through centuries as a heartland of the Atlantic slave trade and a slow colonial conquest, to a hard-won independence and an oil-rich modern republic forged out of decades of war.", terralore.co/country/AGO/chronicle#ev-1500-rise-of-ndongo-under-the-ngola, claim TL:AGO:event:1500:rise-of-ndongo-under-the-ngola, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Ovimbundu and Lunda states take shape
claims.summary: In the central highlands the Ovimbundu kingdoms emerged, while in the east the Lunda states built a wide commercial and political network across the interior savanna.

claims.title: Portuguese found Luanda
claims.summary: Paulo Dias de Novais established São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda on the Angolan coast, creating the base from which Portuguese power and the slave trade would expand.

claims.title: Founding of Benguela
claims.summary: The Portuguese established the port of Benguela to the south, which would become a second major outlet for the export of enslaved Africans to the Americas.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Angola: From the kingdoms of Kongo, Ndongo and Matamba and Queen Njinga's long resistance, through centuries as a heartland of the Atlantic slave trade and a slow colonial conquest, to a hard-won independence and an oil-rich modern republic forged out of decades of war.", terralore.co/country/AGO/chronicle#ev-1617-founding-of-benguela, claim TL:AGO:event:1617:founding-of-benguela, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Njinga becomes queen of Ndongo
claims.summary: After leading a diplomatic mission to the Portuguese in 1621, Njinga Mbande took the throne of Ndongo, beginning a decades-long struggle against Portuguese expansion.

sources.label: Njinga a Mbande: Power and War in 17th-Century Angola
sources.publisher: Oxford Research Encyclopedia of African History

claims.title: Njinga rules from Matamba
claims.summary: Driven from Ndongo by the Portuguese, Njinga rebuilt her power in the eastern kingdom of Matamba, from which she resisted, raided and negotiated with the colonisers until peace in 1656.

claims.title: Atlantic slave trade at its height
claims.summary: Luanda became the leading slave-trading port of the entire Atlantic, funnelling vast numbers of captives seized in interior wars to the Americas, overwhelmingly to Brazil.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Angola: From the kingdoms of Kongo, Ndongo and Matamba and Queen Njinga's long resistance, through centuries as a heartland of the Atlantic slave trade and a slow colonial conquest, to a hard-won independence and an oil-rich modern republic forged out of decades of war.", terralore.co/country/AGO/chronicle#ev-1641-atlantic-slave-trade-at-its-height, claim TL:AGO:event:1641:atlantic-slave-trade-at-its-height, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Portugal abolishes the slave trade
claims.summary: Portugal formally outlawed the transatlantic slave trade, ending Luanda's centuries as a slaving port, though clandestine traffic and later forced labour persisted in Angola.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Angola: From the kingdoms of Kongo, Ndongo and Matamba and Queen Njinga's long resistance, through centuries as a heartland of the Atlantic slave trade and a slow colonial conquest, to a hard-won independence and an oil-rich modern republic forged out of decades of war.", terralore.co/country/AGO/chronicle#ev-1836-portugal-abolishes-the-slave-trade, claim TL:AGO:event:1836:portugal-abolishes-the-slave-trade, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Berlin Conference and the Scramble
claims.summary: The Berlin Conference required Portugal to demonstrate effective occupation of Angola, spurring the military campaigns that would subdue the independent interior kingdoms.

claims.summary: Portuguese forces conquered the Ovimbundu kingdoms of the central highlands, bringing one of Angola's largest peoples under colonial control.

claims.summary: Heavy fighting against the Kwanhama (Ovambo) in the south marked the violent and protracted character of the Portuguese conquest of Angola's interior frontier.

claims.title: Effective occupation completed
claims.summary: Only in the early twentieth century, with pacification campaigns continuing into the 1920s, did Portugal establish effective control over the whole of Angola.

claims.title: Revolt breaks out
claims.summary: The Baixa de Cassanje cotton workers' revolt, the 4 February attack on a Luanda prison, and the UPA's 15 March uprising in the north marked the start of Angola's war of independence against Portugal.

claims.summary: A ceasefire under the Bicesse Accords legalised UNITA as a party and set the stage for multiparty elections, briefly raising hopes of an end to the war.

claims.title: Disputed elections and renewed war
claims.summary: The MPLA's dos Santos led UNITA's Savimbi in Angola's first multiparty elections, but Savimbi rejected the result and returned to war, plunging the country back into conflict.

claims.title: Death of Savimbi ends the war
claims.summary: Jonas Savimbi was killed in an ambush by government forces; within weeks UNITA and the MPLA signed the Luena Memorandum, ending the twenty-seven-year civil war.
